title: A spiral snowflake
caption: Spiral galaxy NGC 6814, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: NGC 6814 · constellation Aquila · about 75 million light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: A brilliant nucleus sits at the heart of this face-on spiral galaxy, its sweeping arms rippled with intricate dark dust patterns and sprinkled with blue stars. This is NGC 6814, photographed by Hubble. Spiral and irregular galaxies together make up about 60% of the galaxies in the local Universe, yet like snowflakes no two spirals are alike.

That very bright nucleus is a telltale sign that NGC 6814 is a Seyfert galaxy, a type with an active center that can emit strong bursts of radiation. Its core is a highly variable source of X-rays, which leads scientists to suspect a supermassive black hole there, weighing in at about 18 million times the mass of the Sun.
Along the spiral arms lie many regions of ionized gas. A recent burst of star birth in these big clouds has forged the brilliant blue stars seen dotted across the galaxy.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (2.62 x 2.62 arcminutes) and distance (75 million light years), the frame spans roughly 57,000 × 57,000 light-years. Its light set out about 75 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3, using visible and near-infrared filters. The color assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: The near-infrared light included here is invisible to the eye, and the long exposure reveals fine dust detail far beyond what an eye could see.
